# The Value Illusion {#sec-illusion}

Copy-on-modify feels like a magic trick because a 5 GB data frame can
lose one cell and the machine does not blink. The feeling is accurate.
The explanation is ordinary, once you are willing to look at three
mechanisms that were built decades apart and happen to serve the same
illusion.

The public rule: ordinary objects behave as values. Binding a new name
does not copy. Modifying through one name does not change the other name.
The private rule: nodes are shared until a write, and a write copies only
when the reference count says someone else still cares.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  bind[Another name is bound] --> share[Same node, count goes up]
  share --> read[A read]
  read --> share
  share --> write{Write, and is the count above 1?}
  write -->|yes| dup[Duplicate, then mutate the copy]
  write -->|no| inplace[Mutate this node]
  dup --> readers[Other names keep the old node]
  inplace --> readers2[There were no other names]
```

That is {{< glossary "copy-on-modify" >}}. It is not a copy on every
touch, and it is not mutation of a shared value. It is a copy at the
moment a write would otherwise be visible through a second name.

## From NAMED to a real count

Before R 4.0 the bit that answered "may I mutate this?" was `NAMED`, and
it was a terrible counter. It went up to 2 and almost never came back
down. A value that had ever been shared stayed "maybe shared" forever, so
later writes copied even when every other holder had already gone away.
Luke Tierney's
[notes on reference counting](https://developer.r-project.org/Refcnt.html)
are the design argument, written while the new scheme was still something
you compiled in with `SWITCH_TO_REFCNT`. They are a historical document
with a living conclusion. Read them as the motivation, then look at a
modern dump: `REF(n)` is the count, and the macros in `Defn.h` increment
and decrement it at the same assignments that maintain the generational
write barrier.

The write barrier is the part worth understanding, because it explains why
the bookkeeping is affordable. A generational collector has to notice when
an old node grows a pointer to a young one, or the young one gets
collected while the old one still needs it. Those assignment sites already
existed. Reference counting hitchhiked on them: store a new pointer,
increment the new target, decrement the old one. The value illusion is
what that bookkeeping buys the user.

A few holders deliberately do not count. Tierney lists `.Last.value`, the
left-hand side of a complex assignment, and some internal argument lists
built with `CONS_NR` so that merely *calling* a function does not pin the
arguments into permanent sharing. This is why a count is not a moral fact
about your code. It is a census of whoever the runtime and the IDE have
chosen to track.

The practical consequences, all visible from user level and spelled out in
[Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/names-values.html):

- `x <- y` shares. `tracemem` or `lobstr::obj_addr` will agree.
- `y[1] <- 0` on a shared atomic vector allocates a new vector for `y`.
- Replacing one column of a data frame duplicates the list of columns and
  the one column you replaced. The other columns keep their addresses.
  That is the 5 GB frame that "copies" without copying 5 GB.
- A count of 1 means the runtime believes you are the only holder, and a
  primitive is allowed to modify the node in place. This is a promise
  about the implementation, not a license to depend on in-place behavior
  in package code unless you are writing C and have checked the count
  yourself.

Environments do not play this game. Assigning into an environment mutates
the frame. `duplicate1` in the runtime returns an environment unchanged,
in the same group as Nil, symbols, external pointers, and weak references.
The reference count still tells you how many names point at *that
environment*. It does not trigger a duplicate-on-write of the bindings.
Chambers says the contradiction on purpose, in
[*S, R, and Data Science*](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2020-028/):
an environment is accessed by reference, "which deliberately contradicts
the usual non-reference semantics of S," and the same computation "might
have different results if that object was an environment on one hand or a
list with the same elements corresponding to the same names on the other."
That is the warning the dumps are a photograph of. An environment with `REF(11)` is a popular handle, not a value
that is about to be copied for your safety. The global environment is
saturated and locked because it is part of the process.

## ALTREP is the same idea, one floor down

Reference counting avoids copies of data you already materialized.
{{< glossary "ALTREP" >}} avoids materializing the data.

The design note by Tierney, Becker, and Kalibera,
[ALTREP: Alternative Representations for R Objects](https://svn.r-project.org/R/branches/ALTREP/ALTREP.html),
is the primary source, with the 2017 DSC slides and the 2018 tech note
listed from
[developer.r-project.org](https://developer.r-project.org/TechDocs/).
The goal is representational freedom under a stable `SEXPTYPE`. To
existing C code an ALTREP integer still looks like an `INTSXP`. The
payload can be something else:

- a compact arithmetic sequence, so `1:1e9` does not allocate a billion
  integers
- a deferred conversion of strings
- a memory-mapped or distributed vector
- metadata such as "sorted" or "no NAs," so a later question can be
  answered without a scan
- in the original sketch, even an alternative shape for environments

The abstract classes (`ALTREP`, `ALTVEC`, `ALTINTEGER`, `ALTREAL`,
`ALTSTRING`, …) are fixed to the existing type tags. There is no user
hierarchy of representations. A method can return a C `NULL` to mean
"fall back to the ordinary protocol," which is why the feature could land
in a thirty-year-old interpreter. `Dataptr_or_null` is the polite
question: give me the data if it is already here, and do not allocate if
it is not. `Extract_subset` is how a slice of a compact sequence stays
compact.

This is the same family of idea as a buffer protocol or a view: the type
tag is the contract, the bytes are a choice. It is also why "I assigned
`1:n` and the memory graph did not move" is not evidence that R is
reference-semantic. It is evidence that the sequence was never a pile of
boxes to begin with. Force the payload --- `inspect` is often enough, or
any operation that needs a real data pointer --- and the boxes appear.

The `alt` bit in the header is the flag. Combined with the allocation
class, it tells you whether you are looking at a node that owns bytes or
a node that knows how to produce them.

## Promises are the calling convention

Arguments are not passed as values. They are passed as
{{< glossary "promise" >}}s: a `PROMSXP` holding the expression, the
environment in which to evaluate it, and eventually the value. The manual
states the lifecycle in one sentence. Once the promise has been forced,
the environment pointer is set to `NULL` and the value is remembered.
Force-once. After that, the argument is just a value with a history.

That is why the public phrase "pass by value" is a description of the
illusion, not of the calling convention. The convention is: pass by
promise, share until a write, duplicate if the count says the write would
leak. Laziness here is not Haskell's laziness. Haskell delays evaluation
to keep expressions referentially transparent and to permit infinite
structures. R delays evaluation so that a plot can use the expression you
typed as a label, so that a default argument can mention another argument,
and so that non-standard evaluation has something to capture. The cost is
evaluation-order surprises. The benefit is the part of the REPL that feels
like talking.

Specials and builtins are the exception that proves the rule, and they
get their own section in @sec-in-context. A special does not even build
the promises. It receives the arguments raw.

## `<<-` is mutation with the receiver left blank

The discomfort with `<<-`, set next to the comfort with environments, is
not hypocrisy once you separate mutation from *finding the thing you
mutate*.

`<<-` walks the enclosure chain, the same walk a free variable uses on the
way out, and assigns into the first binding it finds, or into the global
environment if it finds none. The target depends on who enclosed the
function. Move the function, wrap it, `local()` it, put it in a package
namespace, and the walk can land somewhere else. The mutation is real.
The receiver is implicit. That is a fragile API even when the memory
model is doing exactly what it was asked.

An explicit environment, or an R6 object, or an S7 object whose parent is
`class_environment`, names the receiver. Aliases see the same mutation
because identity is the point. You can pass the handle, fake it in a
test, and refuse to let a helper go fishing in its parents. Both
techniques modify shared state. One of them puts the shared state in the
signature.

The social rule "never use `<<-`" is a documentation rule that got
promoted to a moral one. The memory-model rule underneath it is better:
do not mutate through a search. If identity matters, hold the object. If
identity does not matter, return a value and let copy-on-modify do its
job.

Haskell's `ST` monad is the typed version of the same instinct. The paper
is Launchbury and Peyton Jones, "Lazy Functional State Threads" (POPL
1994): you may mutate inside a scope, and `runST` will not let the
mutable references escape, so the outside world still sees a pure
function. R can imitate the pattern --- scratch environment in, list or
S7 value out --- and has no type system that can enforce the boundary.
The fence is a convention you write down. Package code that returns the
handle by accident has broken the fence, and nothing in the language will
clear its throat.

## What the illusion is for

The illusion is for reasoning. A function that takes a data frame and
returns a data frame can be read as a transformation of a value, even
though the columns you did not touch are shared and the sequence you did
not expand is still compact. Tests can compare values. Pipes can be
reread. Names do not secretly observe each other's later assignments.

The illusion is a lie for exactly the objects where observation is the
feature: environments, external pointers, weak references, and reference
classes built on top of them. Chambers' principles say everything is an
object and everything that happens is a function call. They do not say
every object has value semantics. The dumps are where you learn which
objects opted out. Designing as if they all opted in, or as if none of
them did, is how packages get either haunted state or tragic performance.
